title: The New Era of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Protection for Infants: A Mini Review of Current Tools for Immunoprophylaxis

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; Orthopneumovirus hominis, including RSV-A and RSV-B) immunoprophylaxis for infants, focusing on the central question of the efficacy, safety, and impact of recently introduced prophylactic strategies.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This narrative review synthesizes published literature with emphasis on pivotal clinical trials, regulatory documents, and recent real-world evidence; eligibility criteria and selection methods are not explicitly reported.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Three immunoprophylaxis products for infants have been approved since 2022: two long-acting monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab and clesrovimab) and a maternal RSV vaccine, with efficacy ranging from 49% to 76% against medically attended RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infections and 55% to 91% against hospitalization due to RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not report heterogeneity in efficacy estimates by geographic region, socioeconomic status, or high-risk subgroups, nor does it address long-term safety beyond initial approval phases.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Post-licensure effectiveness studies should prioritize monitoring durability of protection, safety in preterm infants, and implementation strategies in low-resource settings to optimize global RSV burden reduction.

analysis.summary_en: This mini-review evaluates recent advances in infant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunoprophylaxis, focusing on two long-acting monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab and clesrovimab) and a maternal RSV vaccine approved since 2022. Across pivotal trials and real-world evidence, efficacy against medically attended RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infections ranges from 49% to 76%, and against hospitalization from 55% to 91%, with favorable safety profiles. These interventions have been implemented in multiple countries and have substantially reduced infant RSV burden. Key gaps include limited data on long-term safety, durability of protection, and effectiveness across diverse populations and settings.

title: Maternal RSVpreF Vaccine Effectiveness Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Hospitalized Infants

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of hospitalization in infants, and prior to 2025, no maternal vaccination strategy existed in Australia to prevent RSV disease in this vulnerable population. The study was needed to quantify the effectiveness of a newly introduced maternal RSV prefusion F protein-based vaccine (RSVpreF) in preventing infant RSV hospitalization.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective case-control study with a test-negative design was conducted across 9 hospitals in Australia, enrolling infants born at 28 weeks' gestation or later who were hospitalized with acute respiratory illness (ARI) at 6 months of age or younger between March 1, 2025, and February 28, 2026.
analysis.methods: Vaccine effectiveness (VE) was estimated using logistic regression with confounder adjustment, calculating VE as (1 - adjusted odds ratio) × 100% against hospitalization for RSV lower respiratory tract disease (RSV-LRTD), severe RSV-LRTD, and RSV-ARI.
analysis.main_results: Among 1012 infants hospitalized with ARI, VE against RSV-LRTD hospitalization was 77.8% (95% CI, 66.4%-85.3%) overall, 80.2% (95% CI, 71.1%-86.5%) for infants aged 3 months or younger, 86.3% (95% CI, 79.0%-91.1%) for infants aged 2 months or younger, and 68.2% (95% CI, 42.2%-82.5%) for infants older than 2 months through 4 months of age.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrates high year-round effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination in preventing RSV-associated hospitalization in infants under 6 months, with the highest protection observed in the earliest age intervals. This is the first year-round evaluation of maternal RSVpreF vaccination effectiveness in Australia following its national introduction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the continued use of maternal RSVpreF vaccination as a primary strategy to reduce RSV-related hospitalizations in infants, particularly in the first two months of life when risk is highest.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on hospital-based data, which may not capture all RSV cases in the community. Despite this, the large sample size and consistent VE estimates across multiple outcomes strengthen the evidence. Future analyses with larger sample sizes are planned to evaluate additional subgroups.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of maternal vaccination with the bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein-based vaccine (RSVpreF) in preventing infant RSV hospitalization in Australia. Using a retrospective case-control design with a test-negative approach across nine hospitals, researchers analyzed data from 1,012 infants hospitalized with acute respiratory illness (ARI) aged 6 months or younger between March 2025 and February 2026. Vaccine effectiveness (VE) was calculated using logistic regression with confounder adjustment. The primary outcome, VE against RSV lower respiratory tract disease (RSV-LRTD) hospitalization, was 77.8% overall, with higher protection observed in younger infants (86.3% for those aged 2 months or younger). Comparable VE was found for severe RSV-LRTD (80.4%) and RSV-ARI (80.8%). VE remained consistent across stratifications by gestational age at vaccination and timing of vaccination relative to delivery. The study concludes that maternal RSVpreF vaccination provides high year-round protection against RSV-associated hospitalization in infants under 6 months, particularly in early infancy, supporting its continued use as a national immunization strategy.

title: Papiliotrema Laurentii Bloodstream Infection Following Methylprednisolone Pulse Therapy for Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Associated Acute Encephalopathy in a Child.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Papiliotrema laurentii, an environmental yeast, is increasingly recognized as a cause of invasive infections in immunocompromised individuals, but reports in Japan are limited. The study was needed to document a rare case of Papiliotrema laurentii bloodstream infection in a child receiving methylprednisolone pulse therapy for respiratory syncytial virus-associated acute encephalopathy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a single-patient case report of a 4-year-old Japanese girl with cerebral palsy and epilepsy who developed Papiliotrema laurentii fungemia following methylprednisolone pulse therapy for respiratory syncytial virus-associated acute encephalopathy.
analysis.methods: The isolate was identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry and sequencing of the internal transcribed spacer and D1/D2 regions. Antifungal susceptibility testing was performed, and treatment was adjusted from micafungin to liposomal amphotericin B and later to fosfluconazole based on susceptibility results.
analysis.main_results: Blood cultures performed 3 days after completion of 3-day steroid therapy revealed yeast-like organisms, later confirmed as Papiliotrema laurentii. Antifungal susceptibility testing showed a profile distinct from common yeasts. The patient achieved complete resolution and remained relapse-free at 6-month follow-up.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This is the first reported case of Papiliotrema laurentii fungemia in Japan, highlighting the potential for methylprednisolone pulse therapy to predispose even immunocompetent children to opportunistic fungemia. Accurate identification and susceptibility testing were essential for appropriate antifungal management.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The case underscores the need for heightened clinical awareness of rare fungal pathogens in children receiving immunosuppressive therapies and the importance of precise diagnostic methods to guide antifungal treatment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to a single case report, which restricts generalizability and precludes causal inference. Diagnostic limitations and underreporting may lead to underestimation of Papiliotrema laurentii incidence, warranting improved surveillance and diagnostic capacity.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a 4-year-old Japanese girl with cerebral palsy and epilepsy who developed Papiliotrema laurentii bloodstream infection following methylprednisolone pulse therapy for respiratory syncytial virus-associated acute encephalopathy. The organism was identified using mass spectrometry and sequencing, and antifungal susceptibility testing guided a switch from micafungin to liposomal amphotericin B and fosfluconazole, resulting in clinical resolution and no relapse at 6 months. This is the first reported case of Papiliotrema laurentii fungemia in Japan, suggesting that methylprednisolone pulse therapy may predispose children to opportunistic fungemia. The findings highlight the importance of accurate identification and susceptibility testing for appropriate antifungal management and underscore the need for improved surveillance and diagnostic capacity to detect rare fungal pathogens in immunocompromised patients.

title: Kinetics and characterization of extracellular vesicle release from cells infected with a clinical isolate of respiratory syncytial virus A (ON1 genotype)

analysis.summary_en: This in vitro study investigated extracellular microvesicle (EMV) release from respiratory epithelial cells infected with a clinical RSV-A (ON1 genotype) isolate. title: Respiratory syncytial virus outbreaks in healthcare facilities: A review of the literature.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; Orthopneumovirus hominis, including RSV-A and RSV-B) outbreaks in healthcare facilities, focusing on vulnerable patient populations such as premature neonates, immunosuppressed patients, and elderly residents of long-term care facilities. The central question addresses the transmission dynamics, severity, and control of RSV outbreaks within these settings.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a narrative review that searched PubMed from 2010 to 2025 for articles on RSV outbreaks in healthcare facilities. Eighteen articles presenting 19 outbreaks were included, covering hematology/oncology/transplantation wards (11 outbreaks), neonatal intensive care units (6 outbreaks), and geriatric hospitals/long-term care facilities (2 outbreaks).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RSV outbreaks in healthcare facilities are frequent, often traced to asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic healthcare personnel, and typically last several weeks. The mean attack rate across outbreaks was 26.04% (range: 12.00%-68.96%), with a mean duration of 39.9 days (range: 5-131 days). The overall case fatality rate among infected patients was 11.64%, with higher rates in hematology/oncology/transplantation units (13.99%) compared to neonatal intensive care units (6.49%) and geriatric clinics (6.25%).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Prolonged virus shedding in premature neonates and immunosuppressed patients challenges outbreak containment, and the review highlights gaps in infection control practices. The evidence base is limited to 19 outbreaks across specific high-risk settings, leaving uncertainty about transmission dynamics in other healthcare environments and populations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priority research should investigate the role of asymptomatic healthcare personnel in RSV transmission and evaluate multimodal interventions, including palivizumab prophylaxis, for outbreak control. Enhanced surveillance and infection control measures are needed in high-risk units, particularly for elderly and immunocompromised patients, to reduce outbreak severity and mortality.

analysis.summary_en: This review synthesizes evidence on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) outbreaks in healthcare facilities, focusing on vulnerable populations such as premature neonates, immunosuppressed patients, and elderly residents. Across 19 outbreaks, RSV demonstrated high attack rates (mean 26.04%) and prolonged durations (mean 39.9 days), with healthcare personnel often serving as asymptomatic sources. The overall case fatality rate was 11.64%, with the highest burden in hematology/oncology/transplantation units. Key gaps include challenges in containing outbreaks due to prolonged shedding in high-risk patients and limited evidence from diverse healthcare settings. Research priorities include investigating transmission dynamics, evaluating multimodal interventions like palivizumab, and strengthening infection control in high-risk units.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Adults in India: An Under-recognized Public Health Concern Demanding Urgent Immunization Action.

analysis.research_question_and_background: RSV is a major global cause of acute respiratory tract infections with substantial morbidity and mortality across all age groups, yet its burden in older adults and in India remains under-characterized and under-recognized. The study addresses the knowledge gap regarding RSV disease burden among Indian adults and the regulatory status of adult RSV vaccines.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a narrative review that synthesizes existing evidence on RSV burden in Indian adults and evaluates the regulatory landscape of adult RSV vaccines. It focuses on hospitalized adults, particularly older adults with comorbidities, and discusses surveillance priorities and policy needs in India.
analysis.methods: The review integrates published evidence on RSV epidemiology in adults, regulatory approvals of RSV vaccines in other regions, and real-world effectiveness data from the United Kingdom. It proposes integration of routine RSV molecular testing, inclusion of RSV vaccination in national immunization deliberations, and implementation of multicenter studies to generate robust evidence.
analysis.main_results: The review highlights that RSV contributes substantially to severe acute respiratory infections in hospitalized Indian adults, with a notable burden among older adults. It notes that three vaccines (GSK Arexvy, Pfizer Abrysvo, Moderna mRNA-1345) are approved for adults aged 60 years and older in the United States and Europe, and that India has conditionally approved Phase III trials for RSVPreF but no adult RSV vaccine is currently licensed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as evidence that RSV in Indian adults is under-recognized and likely underestimated, particularly in high-risk groups, and emphasize the urgent need for strengthened surveillance, policy integration, and vaccine deployment. The novelty lies in synthesizing Indian-specific gaps and proposing actionable steps for surveillance and immunization.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support prioritizing RSV molecular testing in comorbid adults, including RSV vaccination in national immunization policy deliberations, and accelerating regulatory pathways leveraging global data to inform health technology assessment and cost-effectiveness analyses in India.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence base relies on a narrative review of limited national adult-specific data from India, which constrains generalizability and precision. analysis.summary_en: This narrative review examines the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among adults in India, highlighting its under-recognition and substantial contribution to severe acute respiratory infections, particularly in older adults with comorbidities. The authors synthesize evidence on RSV epidemiology, regulatory approvals of adult RSV vaccines in other regions, and real-world effectiveness data, noting that three vaccines are approved for adults aged 60 years and older in the United States and Europe. In India, Phase III trials for RSVPreF have been conditionally approved, but no adult RSV vaccine is currently licensed. The review emphasizes the urgent need for strengthened surveillance, integration of RSV molecular testing in high-risk groups, inclusion of RSV vaccination in national immunization policy deliberations, and accelerated regulatory pathways leveraging global data. While the findings underscore the importance of addressing RSV in Indian adults, the evidence base is limited by scarce national adult-specific data, resulting in a moderate strength of evidence.

title: Live human metapneumovirus vaccine candidates attenuated by temperature sensitivity mutations from human respiratory syncytial virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory illness in young children, and there are no licensed vaccines. Given the similarities between HMPV and the related human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV), the study aimed to develop live-attenuated HMPV vaccine candidates by introducing temperature-sensitivity/attenuating mutations originally developed for HRSV into the HMPV polymerase gene.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study generated live-attenuated HMPV vaccine candidates by introducing temperature-sensitivity/attenuating mutations into the HMPV polymerase (L) ORF, including Δ1238, C1238S/Y1246K, C1238S, and Y1246K. Replication and genetic stability were assessed in Vero cells at 32°C and 37°C, and the immunogenicity and protective efficacy were evaluated in hamsters inoculated intranasally.
analysis.methods: HMPV vaccine candidates were engineered by introducing HRSV-derived temperature-sensitivity/attenuating mutations into the HMPV L ORF, including Δ1238 (corresponding to HRSV Δ1313/I1314L) and C1238S/Y1246K (corresponding to HRSV “1030s”). Replication kinetics were measured in Vero cells at 32°C and 37°C, and temperature sensitivity was determined by shutoff temperature (T_SH). Genetic stability was assessed under temperature stress, and immunogenicity and protection were evaluated in hamsters after intranasal inoculation.
analysis.main_results: At 37°C, replication of Δ1238, C1238S/Y1246K, and Y1246K was delayed, with peak titers approximately 80-fold, 200-fold, and 25-fold lower than wild-type HMPV, respectively. The C1238S control was not temperature-sensitive (T_SH > 40°C), while Y1246K and Δ1238 (T_SH = 39°C) and C1238S/Y1246K (T_SH = 38°C) exhibited a temperature-sensitive phenotype. The C1238S/Y1246K and Δ1238 candidates were restricted in replication in hamsters but were immunogenic and protective against HMPV challenge.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The introduction of HRSV-derived temperature-sensitivity/attenuating mutations into the HMPV L ORF generated live-attenuated HMPV vaccine candidates that are temperature-sensitive, attenuated, genetically stable, immunogenic, and protective in a hamster model. This approach leverages previously validated HRSV mutations, demonstrating a novel strategy for HMPV vaccine development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the advancement of live-attenuated HMPV vaccine candidates to pediatric clinical studies, offering a potential solution to the unmet need for HMPV vaccination in young children. The genetically stable temperature-sensitive mutations provide a robust platform for further development and evaluation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in vitro and in a hamster model, which may not fully recapitulate human infection or immune responses. While the temperature-sensitive mutations were genetically stable under temperature stress, their stability and safety in humans remain to be confirmed. The evidence strength is moderate due to the preclinical nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed live-attenuated human metapneumovirus (HMPV) vaccine candidates by introducing temperature-sensitivity/attenuating mutations originally derived from human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) into the HMPV polymerase gene. Engineered candidates, including Δ1238 and C1238S/Y1246K, exhibited temperature-sensitive replication in vitro, with peak titers at 37°C reduced by 25- to 200-fold compared to wild-type HMPV. In hamsters, these candidates were restricted in replication yet induced immunogenicity and protection against HMPV challenge. The mutations were genetically stable under temperature stress, supporting their suitability for clinical development. These findings highlight a novel strategy for HMPV vaccine design, leveraging validated HRSV attenuating mutations, and justify advancing the candidates to pediatric vaccine studies.

title: Household Transmission Dynamics of Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus in China: A Multicentre Epidemiological and Molecular Study.

title: The outpatient economic burden of respiratory syncytial virus infection in adults aged ≥ 60 years in Germany: results from the BUCOSS study

title: The limitations of non-mechanistic methods for characterizing pathogen-pathogen interactions: A simulation study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Pathogen-pathogen interactions influence the risk of infection or disease from one pathogen due to another, and such interactions are increasingly recognized as common in infectious disease epidemiology. The study highlights a knowledge gap regarding the reliability of non-mechanistic statistical methods for inferring causality from time-series data in this context.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study performed a simulation-based evaluation of four non-mechanistic methods—generalized additive models (GAMs), Granger causality, transfer entropy, and convergent cross-mapping (CCM)—using synthetic outbreak datasets generated from a two-pathogen mechanistic transmission model calibrated to resemble influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) dynamics.
analysis.methods: Synthetic datasets were created with varying interaction strengths and durations using a mechanistic model, and each method was applied to all datasets to assess their ability to infer interaction presence and strength. The methods were also tested on two real-world datasets from Hong Kong and Canada.
analysis.main_results: Granger causality, transfer entropy, and CCM frequently failed to correctly identify interactions, with average sensitivities of 80.6%, 92.1%, and 72.1% and specificities of 31.0%, 33.3%, and 33.1%, respectively. GAMs performed better, with sensitivity of 85.2% and specificity of 72.5%, and showed larger point estimates for stronger interactions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors conclude that accurately characterizing pathogen-pathogen interactions from outbreak data remains challenging, as most methods struggle to distinguish true interactions from noise. GAMs showed comparatively better performance but still had limited utility, particularly in assessing interaction asymmetry.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution against using unvalidated non-mechanistic methods to infer pathogen-pathogen interactions, which could lead to misleading conclusions with implications for surveillance and epidemic control strategies. Rigorous evaluation of methods is essential before applying them to real-world data.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on simulated data and the inability of GAMs to evaluate interaction asymmetry. The evidence strength is moderate due to the abstract-only scope and the lack of real-world validation beyond two datasets, though the simulation framework provides controlled comparisons.

analysis.summary_en: This simulation study evaluated four non-mechanistic methods—GAMs, Granger causality, transfer entropy, and CCM—for inferring pathogen-pathogen interactions using synthetic datasets calibrated to influenza and RSV dynamics. Granger causality, transfer entropy, and CCM frequently misidentified interactions, while GAMs performed better but still showed limited utility, particularly in assessing interaction asymmetry. The authors conclude that accurately characterizing interactions from outbreak data remains challenging and emphasize the need for rigorous method validation before drawing conclusions that could impact surveillance or epidemic control.

The approach offers new insights into causal evaluation by addressing limitations of traditional pre-post designs, which can confound changes in epidemic timing with shifts in disease burden.
